title: Kirtan at home
hook: many families sing a shabad in the evening or before sleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sangat singing back, the room answering the ragis. Your line was voices together. Did other voices carry yours? Day one hundred thirteen.

Every home has its evening sounds. The TV murmuring in another room. A dishwasher. Someone scrolling, someone arguing about homework, a phone buzzing on the counter long after anyone should be answering it. In many Punjabi homes, the evening has another sound. A grandmother, sitting on the edge of her bed, singing a shabad softly as the lights go off. A father with a small harmonium on the living room rug, a child next to him, both a little out of tune. Or just a phone on the nightstand playing a hymn quietly while someone falls asleep. The gurdwara has its own evening programs. The home has every night.
screen: `THE TV IN THE NEXT ROOM.` → `A SHABAD AS THE LIGHTS GO OFF.` → `THE HOME IS EVERY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: For nine days you've been learning kirtan: listening, the raag, the instruments, the rahao, reading along, humming, Waheguru, one line, the sangat. Today it comes home. Sikh daily life has an evening shape. The Sikh code of conduct sets Rehras Sahib, the evening prayer, for sunset. And last thing at night, before sleep, comes Kirtan Sohila, a short set of five shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib. Its very name has kirtan in it: sohila is a song of praise, a song of joy. It's the same prayer sung when the Granth is put to rest in the gurdwara at night, and at the end of a Sikh funeral. So the day, and the scripture, and a life, all close with it. Remember the line you met on day ninety-six? That in everyone there is a light, and that light is the One? It comes from Kirtan Sohila. Some Sikh children grow up falling asleep to it. Not every family recites the whole thing aloud together every night. They might sing one shabad after dinner, or play a recording as the house goes quiet, or a parent might sing one line at a bedside. It doesn't need to be polished. It's not a concert. The Gurus lived as householders, and their hymns were sung in kitchens and courtyards long before any grand building. And consider what it does to a home. The last sound of the day isn't the news, or a notification, or an argument. It's a hymn. The rooms fill up with it. Over years, some children remember it the way others remember a lullaby. This closes the kirtan days. Tomorrow, langar.
screen: `NINE DAYS, NOW COMING HOME.` · `REHRAS AT SUNSET.` · `KIRTAN SOHILA BEFORE SLEEP.` · `THE LAST SOUND OF THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE HOME FILLS UP.`

segments.voice: Rehearse tonight now. Picture your room at bedtime: the light, the pillow, the phone on the nightstand. Picture putting the phone face down. Then sing your one line from two days ago, very softly, the way you'd sing to a child who's nearly asleep. Or sing Waheguru, a few times. Let the sound fill the space around you. Then let it fade into quiet, and stay in the quiet. Tonight, do it for real. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan at home. Rehras at sunset, Kirtan Sohila before sleep, and a single shabad sung at a bedside: the Word, living in ordinary houses.
Your line: the home fills up. Tonight, make one line of kirtan the last sound before you sleep. Day one hundred thirteen.
